ABSTRACT: Confinement of hydrocarbons in nanoscale pockets and pores provides tunable capability for controlling molecules in catalysts, sorbents, and membranes for reaction and separation applications. While computation of the enthalpic interactions of hydrocarbons in confined spaces has improved, understanding and predicting the entropy of confined molecules remains a challenge. Here we show, using a set of nine aluminosilicate zeolite frameworks with broad variation in pore and cavity structure, that the entropy of adsorption can be predicted as a linear combination of rotational and translational entropy. The extent of entropy lost upon adsorption is predicted using only a single material descriptor, the occupiable volume ( $ V_{occ} $). Predictive capability of confined molecular entropy permits an understanding of the relation with adsorption enthalpy, the ability to computationally screen microporous materials, and an understanding of the role of confinement on the kinetics of molecules in confined spaces.

On the basis of this shape-selective feature , highly effective molecular separations and selective catalytic conversions can be achieved within zeolitic structures that are difficult to accomplish with other materials and/or techniques . $ ^ { 1-3 } $ So far, several shape-selectivity mechanisms have been elucidated and applications identified. $ ^{2-18} $ In common molecular sieving, bulky molecules adsorb preferentially over bulkier species as a result of steric constraints imposed by the zeolites' framework, e.g., linear alkane molecules compared to branched isomers. $ ^{19-23} $ Besides this common adsorption competition based on molecular bulkiness, the reverse phenomenon can also occur, i.e., competitive adsorption in favor of the bulkier species. The enthalpy and the entropy contributions to the Gibbs free energies were calculated at T = 298 K and partial pressure of 1 atm (101325 Pa). The enthalpy (H) of gas-phase pyridine and acetonitrile molecules is defined as the sum of total electronic energy ( $ E_{el} $), internal vibrational energy ( $ E_{v} $), zero-point vibrational energy (ZPVE), as well as the rotational and translational contributions to the internal energy: $ H = E_{el} + E_{v} + ZPVE + E_{R} + E_{t} $. The corresponding calculated entropies (S) includes translational, ( $ S_{t} $) vibrational, ( $ S_{v} $) and rotational ( $ S_{r} $) degrees of freedom: $ S = S_{t} + S_{v} + S_{r} $. All the considered systems are in singlet state, thus the electronic contribution to the entropy is zero. The first attempts to describe guest-induced flexibility in zeolites were done using molecular dynamics simulations. $ ^{79-82} $ Rigid zeolitic force fields were dynamically modified using transition state theory to include lattice flexibility, and the results obtained by these models were in good agreement with experimental data. $ ^{79-81,83,84} $ It was shown that framework flexibility in silicalite-1 (MFI-type framework) is responsible for the adsorption of large molecules such as isobutane and heptane with inflection behavior at high loadings, $ ^{80} $ while enhanced self-diffusivity at low loadings of short alkanes (i.e. methane and n-butane) was observed. $ ^{81} $ Framework flexibility is also crucial for aromatics adsorption on MFI zeolite, especially at high pressures. $ ^{84,85} $ While the use of rigid zeolitic models led to the underestimation of the aromatics adsorption in MFI zeolite by a factor of two, $ ^{84,85} $ the use of flexible models to simulate diffusion coefficients of various alkanes in silicalite-1 zeolite resulted in a convergence of experimental and theoretical values. $ ^{86} $ Recently by using in situ integrated differential phase contrast scanning transmission electron microscopy (iDPC-STEM) while adsorbing benzene molecules on MFI zeolite, Xiong et al. showed that the MFI structure goes through severe deformations giving another proof of guest-induced flexibility in zeolites (see Fig. 4). $ ^{87} $

2.4.4. Trapdoor. Traditional diﬀusion models primarily consider two types of interactions: those between guest molecules (guest–guest) and those between guest molecules and the zeolite framework (guest–host). However, when cations are present in the zeolite structure, a third interaction—involving guest molecules, the framework, and cations (guest–host-cation)—must also be accounted for. A striking example of such ternary interactions is the well-known ‘‘molecular trapdoor’’. This phenomenon, also referred to as the ‘‘gating effect’’, describes a unique molecular sieving mechanism in certain zeolites and related porous materi- als. Here, extra-framework cations function as dynamic gate- keepers at pore apertures, selectively controlling molecular diffusion to achieve highly discriminative adsorption and separation.9,147,187 To date, ‘‘trapdoor’’ has been observed in several zeolites, including RHO (DNL-6),188–190 CHA (SAPO-34, SSZ-13),147,191,192 MWF (ZSM-25),149,193 HEU (Clinoptilolite),194

descriptor_candidates.name: confined_shape_stiffness
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss (per R) decreases monotonically as pore-spanning freedom per occupied volume rises: adsorbates in frameworks where the largest pore diameter (lsd_p) is large relative to molecular bounding extent (PBF) and where accessible volume per molecular surface area is high retain more gas-like translational freedom, so a log-linear descriptor of Vol/LabuteASA times lsd_p/PBF improves MAE of s_ads/s_gas prediction over the baseline neural net.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference from E01/E03: entropy loss is dominated by suppression of translation; frameworks with large occupiable volume and wide channels (FAU-like, low loss) vs. tight channels (TON-like, high loss). The ratio Vol/LabuteASA captures free-volume per contact surface; lsd_p/PBF captures fit tightness between molecule and largest pore.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If adding this descriptor to the 14-input baseline does not reduce MAE of entropy loss/R by a pre-specified margin (e.g., >5% on cross-validation), or if residuals show no monotonic trend versus the descriptor, the hypothesis is rejected.

descriptor_candidates.name: anisometry_rotational_lock
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss increases when molecular rotational anisometry is high AND the framework's shortest free-sphere path (lsd_f) is small relative to its largest pore (lsd_p): strongly aspherical molecules confined in narrow, elongated channels lose rotational entropy disproportionately, so this anisometry-confinement product improves predicted s_ads/s_gas beyond the isotropic-volume baseline.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference from E01 (rotational modes as fraction of gas entropy vary by framework) and E09 (molecular symmetry controls motion under confinement): rotational freezing depends on both molecular shape anisometry (PMI3/PMI1) and channel dimensionality/asymmetry (lsd_f/lsd_p), a coupling absent from single-descriptor V_occ models.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If the descriptor's correlation with entropy loss residuals (after the baseline fit) is not statistically significant, or if removing PMI ratios changes MAE by less than measurement uncertainty, the rotational-lock mechanism is unsupported.

descriptor_candidates.name: packing_density_penalty
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss has two separable additive contributions: a framework packing term (source-scale density times molecular volume relative to accessible pore volume AV, capturing framework–guest commensurability) and a molecular elongation term (SPAN/GeDi, capturing how much of the molecule spans the pore and thus how many vibrational/translational modes are frozen), and their additive combination lowers MAE of entropy loss/R relative to the nonlinear baseline using raw inputs.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference from E03 (single descriptor V_occ predicts loss) extended by E05/E08: shape selectivity and framework flexibility/guest fit modulate confinement beyond total volume; density is used on its source numerical scale as a commensurability index with Vol, and SPAN/GeDi measures length-to-width elongation of the guest.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If the two-term descriptor underperforms a single-term variant (e.g., Vol/AV alone) in MAE on held-out frameworks, or if the density-based term's fitted influence is within noise of zero, the additive two-mechanism hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: free_sphere_surface_bottleneck
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss per R decreases when the framework's accessible surface-to-pore-volume ratio (LabuteASA per AV) is small, and this dependence is amplified when the smallest free-sphere path (lsd_f) is large relative to the molecular bounding-sphere diameter (PBF). The product term predicts that entropy loss is dominated by surface-contact friction in the bottlenecks: molecules whose bounding sphere nearly fills the narrowest window (PBF close to lsd_f) suffer a larger additional rotational/translational freeze that scales with the surface-to-volume index, improving MAE of s_ads/s_gas beyond the 14-input baseline.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference (not directly in sources): E03 shows occupiable volume V_occ alone predicts entropy loss, implying surface/volume geometry encodes the confinement mechanism; E01 shows TON-like frameworks with narrow windows give the largest loss. The descriptor couples the aperture bottleneck (lsd_f vs PBF, a molecular-sieving condition like E05's steric constraints) with the surface-area-to-pore-volume ratio, which the raw feature set only provides separately to the network.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Adding this descriptor to the retained baseline (MAE_R = 0.5528) must reduce cross-validated MAE of entropy loss/R by more than 5%; additionally, residuals must correlate monotonically with lsd_f/PBF within the small-lsd_f regime. If the surface/volume term's contribution is within noise of zero, or if MAE does not improve, the bottleneck-friction mechanism is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: asphericity_window_compression
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss per R is governed by two separable factors: (i) the degree of asphericity captured by the second-to-third principal-moment ratio (PMI2/PMI3), which limits orientational microstates, and (ii) an exponential penalty when the product of molecular bounding extent and length-to-width span (PBF*SPAN) exceeds the framework's smallest free path lsd_f. Molecules that are both aspherical and geometrically compressed by the narrowest window lose rotational entropy multiplicatively (not additively), so this descriptor improves MAE of entropy loss/R versus the baseline and versus the retained anisometry_rotational_lock descriptor.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence: E09 reports that molecular symmetry controls rotational/translational motion under confinement (correlated bond-vector rotation in AFI/VFI/MAZ). E06 shows adsorbed-molecule entropies require reduced translational and rotational contributions when constrained in zeolite cavities. Inference: the multiplicative (exponential) form tests whether shape-confinement effects couple multiplicatively rather than linearly, a distinction the baseline nonlinear net cannot isolate from raw PMIs alone.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: The descriptor must reduce cross-validated MAE of entropy loss/R by >5% relative to MAE_R = 0.5528. Ablating the exponential window-compression factor or replacing PMI2/PMI3 with 1 should each degrade MAE significantly; if neither ablation matters, the multiplicative symmetry-window mechanism is unsupported and the descriptor rejected.

descriptor_candidates.name: elongation_pore_geometry_mismatch
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss per R increases with the product of (i) molecular elongation relative to the largest pore (SPAN/lsd_p), capturing how much of the molecule's length must be accommodated even in its widest channel, and (ii) a framework compaction index (density*Vol/ASA, on source numerical scales for density), capturing how densely packed the framework is per unit accessible surface. Long molecules in compact frameworks lose the most entropy; the interaction term predicts framework compaction amplifies the elongation penalty, improving MAE of entropy loss/R beyond the baseline.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence: E01 shows TON-like 1D narrow-channel frameworks cause the largest entropy loss while FAU (large cavities, lower compaction) causes the smallest; E05 documents shape selectivity from steric mismatch of elongated (linear) molecules in tubular pores. Inference: SPAN/lsd_p quantifies that mismatch, while density*Vol/ASA serves as a compaction/commensurability index (using density only on its native scale, per instructions); their product tests an interaction absent from the retained lsd_f/lsd_p descriptor, which only used the framework-side ratio.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Cross-validated MAE of entropy loss/R must drop by >5% versus the retained baseline (0.5528). If the interaction term underperforms a variant using only SPAN/lsd_p, or if the compaction factor's influence is within measurement noise, the compaction-amplification hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: vibrational_pocket_commensurability
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss per R grows log-linearly with the ratio of molecular volume to accessible pore volume, amplified by the square of the bottleneck mismatch PBF/lsd_f: as the molecule nearly fills both the pore volume and the narrowest window, vibrational amplitudes (librational modes replacing translation/rotation, per E06's reduced rotational/translational corrections) are frozen in a manner quadratic in the geometric fit, not linear. This descriptor predicts the fit-tightness exponent is closer to 2 than 1.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence: E03 (occupiable volume V_occ alone predicts entropy loss) and E06 (adsorbed-molecule rotational/translational contributions reduced when constrained in cavities). Inference: the square of PBF/lsd_f tests whether window-fitting enters the entropy loss quadratically (cage rattling ~ (gap)^-2) rather than linearly; the ratio Vol/AV rescales E03's V_occ by molecular size rather than framework size alone.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Adding this descriptor to the retained baseline (MAE_R = 0.5519) must reduce cross-validated MAE of entropy loss/R by >5%. If the squared form does not outperform a linear PBF/lsd_f variant, or if the Vol/AV term's contribution is within noise, the quadratic-commensurability mechanism is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: inertial_mass_channel_dimensionality
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss per R increases when the molecular mass-per-occupied-volume ratio (MW/(density*Vol), a measure of how much mass the framework must immobilize per unit pore space) is combined with the pore anisotropy ratio lsd_p/lsd_f: frameworks with strongly differing largest-pore and smallest-path dimensions (quasi-1D channels) restrict translational diffusion to fewer effective dimensions, and this restriction matters most for heavy molecules (Sackur–Tetrode translational entropy scales with mass, E01). The descriptor tests whether channel dimensionality and molecular mass interact, which raw inputs supplied separately cannot express.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence: E01 gives the Sackur–Tetrode mass dependence of translational entropy and shows TON-like 1D frameworks cause the largest loss. Inference: effective dimensionality of diffusion is captured by lsd_p/lsd_f spread; mass-dependence predicts the entropy penalty is mass-weighted, an interaction the baseline network cannot isolate from raw MW and framework descriptors.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Cross-validated MAE must drop >5% versus 0.5519. If replacing MW by a constant or lsd_p/lsd_f by 1 in ablations does not degrade MAE, or if the descriptor underperforms the retained anisometry_rotational_lock, the mass-dimensionality coupling is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: surface_area_entropic_capacity
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss per R decreases exponentially with the accessible molecular surface per confined volume (LabuteASA*lsd_f/Vol, the local surface-to-free-space ratio at the bottleneck scale) and increases with the framework-scale surface-area-to-pore-volume ratio ASA/AV: adsorbates retain more gas-like entropy when they have more contact-free free volume per surface contact, while frameworks with high internal surface per pore volume impose more wall contacts. The two-scale (molecular vs framework) surface/volume product predicts that entropy loss is controlled by surface-contact frequency at both scales simultaneously.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence: E03 implies surface/volume geometry encodes confinement entropy; E01 shows framework-dependent loss magnitude. Inference: the exponential decay in molecular-scale surface-to-free-volume tests whether configurational (microstate) loss is a rare-event (exponential) rather than linear function, while ASA/AV provides the framework-scale analogue; the raw feature set contains these scales only separately.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: The descriptor must reduce cross-validated MAE of entropy loss/R by >5% versus 0.5519. Ablating either scale (replacing LabuteASA*lsd_f/Vol by 0, or ASA/AV by 1) should each significantly degrade MAE; if neither ablation matters or the full descriptor shows no improvement, the two-scale surface-entropy mechanism is falsified.

candidates.falsification_criteria: Adding this descriptor to the retained baseline (MAE_R = 0.5519) must reduce cross-validated MAE of entropy loss/R by >5%. If the squared form does not outperform a linear PBF/lsd_f variant, or if the Vol/AV term's contribution is within noise, the quadratic-commensurability mechanism is falsified.
candidates.reason: more than 5 percent nonfinite training values

candidates.name: inertial_mass_channel_dimensionality
candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss per R increases when the molecular mass-per-occupied-volume ratio (MW/(density*Vol), a measure of how much mass the framework must immobilize per unit pore space) is combined with the pore anisotropy ratio lsd_p/lsd_f: frameworks with strongly differing largest-pore and smallest-path dimensions (quasi-1D channels) restrict translational diffusion to fewer effective dimensions, and this restriction matters most for heavy molecules (Sackur–Tetrode translational entropy scales with mass, E01). The descriptor tests whether channel dimensionality and molecular mass interact, which raw inputs supplied separately cannot express.
candidates.rationale: Source evidence: E01 gives the Sackur–Tetrode mass dependence of translational entropy and shows TON-like 1D frameworks cause the largest loss. Inference: effective dimensionality of diffusion is captured by lsd_p/lsd_f spread; mass-dependence predicts the entropy penalty is mass-weighted, an interaction the baseline network cannot isolate from raw MW and framework descriptors.
candidates.falsification_criteria: Cross-validated MAE must drop >5% versus 0.5519. If replacing MW by a constant or lsd_p/lsd_f by 1 in ablations does not degrade MAE, or if the descriptor underperforms the retained anisometry_rotational_lock, the mass-dimensionality coupling is falsified.

candidates.name: surface_area_entropic_capacity
candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss per R decreases exponentially with the accessible molecular surface per confined volume (LabuteASA*lsd_f/Vol, the local surface-to-free-space ratio at the bottleneck scale) and increases with the framework-scale surface-area-to-pore-volume ratio ASA/AV: adsorbates retain more gas-like entropy when they have more contact-free free volume per surface contact, while frameworks with high internal surface per pore volume impose more wall contacts. The two-scale (molecular vs framework) surface/volume product predicts that entropy loss is controlled by surface-contact frequency at both scales simultaneously.
candidates.rationale: Source evidence: E03 implies surface/volume geometry encodes confinement entropy; E01 shows framework-dependent loss magnitude. Inference: the exponential decay in molecular-scale surface-to-free-volume tests whether configurational (microstate) loss is a rare-event (exponential) rather than linear function, while ASA/AV provides the framework-scale analogue; the raw feature set contains these scales only separately.
candidates.falsification_criteria: The descriptor must reduce cross-validated MAE of entropy loss/R by >5% versus 0.5519. Ablating either scale (replacing LabuteASA*lsd_f/Vol by 0, or ASA/AV by 1) should each significantly degrade MAE; if neither ablation matters or the full descriptor shows no improvement, the two-scale surface-entropy mechanism is falsified.

interpretation: Replicates vary LLM proposals on one fixed split, not independent datasets. Novelty is unverified.

retained.name: anisometry_rotational_lock
retained.hypothesis: Entropy loss increases when molecular rotational anisometry is high AND the framework's shortest free-sphere path (lsd_f) is small relative to its largest pore (lsd_p): strongly aspherical molecules confined in narrow, elongated channels lose rotational entropy disproportionately, so this anisometry-confinement product improves predicted s_ads/s_gas beyond the isotropic-volume baseline.

retained.name: free_sphere_surface_bottleneck
retained.hypothesis: Entropy loss per R decreases when the framework's accessible surface-to-pore-volume ratio (LabuteASA per AV) is small, and this dependence is amplified when the smallest free-sphere path (lsd_f) is large relative to the molecular bounding-sphere diameter (PBF). The product term predicts that entropy loss is dominated by surface-contact friction in the bottlenecks: molecules whose bounding sphere nearly fills the narrowest window (PBF close to lsd_f) suffer a larger additional rotational/translational freeze that scales with the surface-to-volume index, improving MAE of s_ads/s_gas beyond the 14-input baseline.
